work combines architecture design, prototype deployment, performance benchmarking,
and security assessment. Results show strong prototype-scale feasibility with low-latency
and high-throughput behavior, while also identifying deployment-blocking security gaps
and operational maturity requirements. The thesis contributes an evidence-traceable
path from concept validation to deployment-grade roadmap planning.

1.1 Background and Motivation
Modern cloud infrastructure has enabled global-scale software delivery, but it has also
consolidated computation, storage, and control into a small number of centralized facili-
ties. For many workloads, this model is effective. For others, especially latency-sensitive,
privacy-sensitive, and locality-bound workloads, centralized execution introduces avoid-
able transport delay, dependency on external operators, and persistent cost overhead for
data that is frequently produced and consumed near the edge.
This thesis is motivated by a specific systems question: can high-performance inter-
connect techniques normally associated with specialized datacenter or High-Performance
Computing (HPC) environments be adapted to decentralized, neighborhood-scale infras-
tructure patterns while preserving practical operability? Rather than approaching this
question as pure simulation, the work evaluates it through implemented systems and
measured behavior.
The research context combines technical and translational drivers. Technically, PCIe-
fabric semantics suggest a path to low-latency disaggregated resource sharing beyond
single-host boundaries. Translationally, there is growing pressure to reduce unnecessary
dependence on centralized data-center paths for edge-suitable workloads, while improving
1
data locality and operational sovereignty, as described in my Literature Review (Niccum
2026b) and in my Proposal (Niccum 2026e).
Recent policy and infrastructure analysis also highlights why location and scale de-
cisions matter for host communities. As Walker and Goldsmith describe in their World
Resources Institute analysis, rapid data-center growth can place significant pressure on
local electricity systems and water supplies while introducing additional air-quality and
land-use trade-offs for nearby residents (Walker and Goldsmith 2026). These local re-
source effects were a major motivation for this thesis and reinforce the value of evaluating
distributed, neighborhood-scale alternatives.
1.2 Problem Definition
The target systems studied in this thesis are virtualized and distributed neigh-
borhood data-center models built from PCIe-fabric-inspired resource sharing primi-
tives. Across these models, multiple nodes cooperate to expose storage, memory, and se-
lected device capabilities with lower communication overhead than conventional network-
attached consumer storage workflows.
This concept is distinct from two familiar alternatives:
• They are not traditional standalone home Network-Attached Storage (NAS) de-
signs focused only on local file serving.
• They are not hyperscale cloud replication attempts with global fault domains and
centralized multi-region governance.
Instead, these models occupy a middle architectural space: localized distributed in-
frastructure intended to preserve high-performance resource access properties while re-
maining operationally realistic on non-datacenter hardware.
1.3 Research Questions
RQ1: Can PCIe-fabric-based distributed infrastructure provide cloud-like utility with
lower latency and stronger data locality?
RQ2: Whataretherealperformance, security,andoperationallimitsofcurrentprototype
implementations?
RQ3: How does emerging industry activity (NVIDIA/SPAN) validate, challenge, or redi-
rect this architecture?
RQ4: What changes are required to move from experimental prototype to deployable
market system?

1.4 Scope and Boundaries
The implemented scope of this thesis includes:
• multiple validated multi-node prototype architectures,
• animplementationjourneydocumentingdeploymentconstraintsandresolutionpat-
terns,
• empirical performance characterization across latency/throughput/signaling paths,
• and a security assessment with measured mitigation outcomes.
The work does not claim completion of production-grade neighborhood deployment.
Deferred scope includes fully authenticated segment-access governance, complete fabric
confidentialitycontrols,large-scalefieldvalidationacrossmanyhomes,andcommercialization-
grade operations programs.
Throughout the thesis, claims are bounded accordingly: prototype-level findings are
presented as validated evidence; deployment-roadmap elements are presented as direc-
tional projections.
1.5 Contributions and Claim Boundaries
This thesis contributes in three classes.
Empirical technical contributions. This work provides architecture validation
across multiple PCIe-fabric prototypes, including explicit role and path decomposition
in the implemented three-node topology. It also reports measured performance charac-
teristics, including low-microsecond remote memory latency and high-throughput DMA
transfer behavior in the implemented system.
Security and hardening contributions. This thesis introduces a vulnerability
model tailored to shared residential deployment conditions and reports measured mit-
igation outcomes. These outcomes are presented with explicit implementation status
(implemented, partial, failed, deferred) and overhead impact where available.
Practice-embedded engineering contributions. The thesis contributes a struc-
tured implementation narrative that links real deployment failures to repeatable debug-
ging and operational patterns. It also establishes a practical bridge from infrastructure-
level behavior to application-facing design implications.
Claim boundary statement: this thesis validates prototype-scale feasibility and iden-
tifies concrete hardening requirements. It does not claim that the full neighborhood-scale
market architecture is already production-ready.

1.6 Thesis Roadmap
Chapter 2 establishes the technical and related-work baseline for decentralized and PCIe-
fabric-based systems. It defines the key concepts and prior approaches that frame the
design decisions made later in the thesis. It also clarifies where this work aligns with,
and departs from, existing literature.
Chapter 3 defines the methodological framework, including field-embedded iteration
and evidence traceability. It explains how prototypes, measurements, and operational
observations were collected and validated over time. The chapter also describes how
methodological constraints are handled to keep claims bounded and reproducible.
Chapter 4 presents system architecture with explicit implemented-versus-proposed
separation. It details node roles, communication paths, and the structure of shared
resource exposure in the tested topologies. This chapter establishes the architectural
vocabulary used in the implementation, performance, and security analyses.
Chapter 5 documents implementation realities and operational engineering lessons,
drawing from deployment records and the MySummer synthesis. It traces key build and
integration failures, the debugging process used to resolve them, and the practical con-
straints discovered in non-datacenter environments. The chapter emphasizes repeatable
patterns that can inform future implementations.
Chapter 6 reports empirical performance results and bounded interpretation. It
presents measured latency, throughput, and signaling behavior across the implemented
systems and compares observed outcomes to expected behavior. The analysis distin-
guishes validated findings from preliminary indicators that require larger-scale follow-up.
Chapter 7 analyzes security posture, mitigation outcomes, and residual risk. It eval-
uates threats specific to shared residential and neighborhood-style deployment contexts,
then maps each mitigation to implementation status and overhead. The chapter closes by
identifying unresolved risks and hardening priorities for production-oriented evolution.
Chapter 8 positions the work relative to emerging industry convergence narratives. It
examines where current ecosystem movements, including NVIDIA/SPAN-aligned direc-
tions, validate or challenge the architectural assumptions of this thesis. The chapter uses
this comparison to refine which parts of the approach are most durable.
Chapter 9 extracts practice-embedded insights and confidentiality-bounded lessons
from field engagement. It focuses on decision-making patterns, communication con-
straints, and implementation habits that improved execution quality over time. These
insights are presented as transferable guidance rather than universal prescriptions.
Chapter 10 synthesizes findings, revisits research questions, and separates proven
results from projected pathways. It integrates architectural, performance, security, and
operational evidence into a single interpretation of feasibility and limits. The chapter
explicitly marks where confidence is high and where further validation is still required.

2.1 DistributedandEdgeInfrastructureFoundations
As Datacate emphasizes in its analysis of data center siting, placement matters: where
computation and data are located changes latency, reliability exposure, governance con-
straints, and cost behavior (Unknown 2024). Centralized cloud architectures maximize
scale efficiency and operational standardization, but they also introduce unavoidable de-
pendency on wide-area transport paths and external control domains. Edge computing
emerged as a corrective pattern for locality-sensitive workloads, moving selected compute
and storage closer to data generation and user interaction points (Niccum 2026b).
Inmanydistributednetworkdesigns,complexitysuchasdatapackaging,pre-processing,
and protocol shaping is intentionally handled near the network edge, close to where data
is created and consumed. Large centralized data-center models often break this pattern
by pushing more transformation and coordination into remote core facilities, which can
increase round-trip dependency and reduce local control over timing-sensitive data paths.
The neighborhood-scale perspective in this thesis can be understood as an edge-local
specialization. Instead of placing one lightweight edge node in front of remote cloud
services, the model explores collaborative local infrastructure where nearby participants
share pooled capabilities. This pattern combines two ideas: locality for response and
6
autonomy, and cooperative pooling for efficiency. The related-work baseline therefore
spansdistributedsystems, edgeorchestration, anddecentralizedtrust/operationsmodels.
A key methodological takeaway from this literature is that decentralization is not
automatically beneficial. It can reduce transport delay and improve locality, but it can
also increase management complexity, fault coordination burden, and security surface
area. This tradeoff framing is directly reflected in the evaluation structure of this thesis.
2.2 PCIe Fabrics, RDMA, and Disaggregated Sys-
tems
PCIe and PCIe-derived interconnect approaches provide a different operating point from
Ethernet-first distributed systems. Ethernet-based models, including RDMA over con-
verged networks, offer broad ecosystem compatibility and mature operations tooling. In
a conventional network stack, data commonly traverses multiple software and protocol
boundariesfromapplicationandmiddlewarelayersthroughtransport/networkprocessing
before physical transmission, and each boundary can add latency, buffering, and coor-
dination overhead. Dolphin’s PCIe-fabric software model is designed to reduce portions
of that path for local high-performance sharing by enabling more direct memory and
device-oriented transfer semantics across hosts, bypassing some intermediate networking-
layer processing that is typical in Ethernet-first designs, (Dolphin Interconnect Solutions
2026d; Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026b; Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026c).
SISCI-oriented fabrics and related mechanisms (including memory-segment opera-
tions, high-speed queueing patterns, and device lending semantics) are attractive because
they expose near-bus-like resource interaction patterns across node boundaries. In prac-
tical terms, this supports disaggregation patterns where resources attached to one host
can be consumed by another with reduced data-movement penalties.
Comparedwithlocalbuses, fabricapproachesacceptcoordinationoverheadandtrust-
boundary complexity in exchange for cross-node reachability. Compared with conven-
tional networked alternatives, they may improve locality-sensitive performance but re-
quire tighter integration discipline and stronger hardening in shared environments.
This thesis positions PCIe-fabric concepts as a candidate substrate for decentralized
micro-data-center behavior, then tests that position empirically rather than assuming
transferability from HPC contexts (Niccum 2026a; Niccum 2026b).
2.3 Decentralized Storage and Compute Models
Decentralized storage and compute models include peer-to-peer distribution, federated
clusters, and community infrastructure cooperatives. These models often emphasize re-
7
silience through distribution and local ownership of assets, but they differ in assumptions
about interconnect quality, trust administration, and scheduling.
From these traditions, several ideas are directly transferable to neighborhood-scale
PCIe-fabric exploration. First, role separation between control-plane and data-plane
functions keeps orchestration, policy, and membership decisions isolated from high-speed
data movement paths. In practice, this means that node admission, capability assign-
ment, and coordination logic can evolve without forcing constant changes to low-latency
transfer paths, reducing operational coupling and recovery risk.
Second, explicit membership and identity governance is necessary when shared re-
sources cross household or organizational boundaries. Rather than assuming all partici-
pants are equally trusted, the model needs clear identity verification, scoped permissions,
and revocation paths for segment access and device exposure.
Third, fault-domain design that limits blast radius is essential for real-world resilience.
A local misconfiguration, compromised node, or unstable device should be containable
to a bounded segment so that one failure does not cascade across the full neighborhood
fabric.
Finally, policy-driven fairness mechanisms are required under competing demand,
especially when smaller edge participants may be resource-constrained relative to large
platform actors. Scheduling, quotas, priority classes, and admission controls help ensure
that shared capacity is not monopolized by the most aggressive or best-funded workloads,
preserving predictable service for local users.
Less directly transferable are assumptions that all links are homogeneous, that par-
ticipants use uniform hardware, or that cryptographic and policy controls can be layered
in late without architecture impact. The present thesis confirms that hardware hetero-
geneity and control-surface specifics materially affect both performance and risk posture.
2.4 Pre-Announcement Landscape
Before major recent industry visibility around neighborhood-edge infrastructure narra-
tives, relevant work was fragmented across High-Performance Computing (HPC) inter-
connect engineering, edge computing, distributed storage, and privacy/sovereignty dis-
course. In that pre-announcement landscape, high-performance interconnect technologies
were rarely framed as practical components for small-scale shared community infrastruc-
ture. They were typically discussed in enterprise, lab, or specialized appliance contexts.
This fragmentation created a practical gap: many components existed in isolation
(high-performance transport, local virtualization, edge use-case pressure), but end-to-end
synthesis for residential cooperative deployment was underdeveloped in public technical
literature.
The early premise of this thesis emerged in that gap, prior to strong mainstream
8
signaling that similar architectural themes would become visible in broader industry
narratives.
Today, that premise appears increasingly timely: the field is approaching an inflection
point where decentralization-oriented data-center models are moving from niche exper-
imentation toward broader technical and commercial relevance. Rather than replacing
the internet’s existing architecture in a single transition, these models are more likely to
be woven into current cloud and edge patterns as adoption grows, gradually reshaping
infrastructure design through hybrid integration.
2.5 Research Gap Analysis
The literature and technical baseline reveal five unresolved gaps that motivate this thesis.
Gap1: ThereislimitedempiricalworkconnectingPCIe-fabricconceptstoneighborhood-
scale deployment contexts. Much of the available evidence comes from enterprise, lab,
or specialized High-Performance Computing environments rather than community-scale
infrastructure with mixed ownership and local operational constraints.
Gap 2: There are insufficient implementation narratives describing real operational
blockers on heterogeneous non-datacenter hosts. Existing literature often emphasizes
architecture and performance potential, but provides less detail on practical integration
failures, recovery patterns, and day-to-day deployment friction across mixed systems.
Gap3: Benchmarkevidenceremainssparsewhenarchitecturedecisionsandpractical
transfer behavior are interpreted together for this setting. This is especially important
because the underlying interconnect technology was not traditionally adopted for this
specific neighborhood-scale use case, so assumptions from prior domains do not automat-
ically transfer.
Gap 4: Threat models are underdeveloped for shared residential fabrics where trust
is distributed and attack entry points are mixed. Because this is a newer application
context for this hardware class, node-to-node security boundaries and cooperative trust
controls have not historically been the central focus of most prior deployments.
Gap5: Claim-disciplineboundariesareoftenweakwhenseparatingprototype-proven
findings from strategic projections. Since this research area is still emerging, it is easy
for forward-looking narratives to outrun validated evidence unless claims are explicitly
bounded.
Chapters 3 through 7 are structured to close these gaps systematically: Chapter 3
defines the empirical method and evidence-traceability rules, Chapter 4 specifies the ar-
chitecture, Chapter 5 reports implementation realities, Chapter 6 provides performance
evidence, and Chapter 7 analyzes security risks and mitigation outcomes. This progres-
sion converts an attractive concept into a testable and bounded technical argument.

3.1 Research Paradigm
This thesis follows a systems engineering and design-science style methodology. The work
is not limited to simulation or conceptual modeling; it includes building and validating
a functioning PCIe-fabric prototype, then evaluating that prototype under practical op-
erating conditions. The central research proposition is that PCIe-based resource pooling
can be extended beyond a single workstation or centralized rack-scale deployment and
used as the core of a neighborhood-scale, decentralized micro-data center model.
Methodologically, the emphasis is on empirical evidence from implemented systems.
Performance and security are treated as primary evaluation axes, with energy and cost
considered secondary and directional in this chapter. The chapter therefore focuses on
how the prototype was built, how experiments were structured, which metrics were col-
lected, and how results were interpreted within known system constraints.
The approach is intentionally hybrid in tone and execution: academically structured
enough for research evaluation, but grounded in real deployment behavior observed while
developing and operating the platform.
10
3.2 Prototype-Centered Empirical Method
The core testbed is a multi-node PCIe fabric prototype built with commodity house-
hold computers and specialized PCIe fabric adapter hardware. The baseline valida-
tion platform is a three-node topology, which served as the primary environment for
repeatable experiments. Beyond this baseline, the cluster assembled for this research in-
cludesvalidatedlarger-topologyandexpansion-capableconfigurations, includinguptosix
nodes and shared-fabric device-pooling paths, using MXH930 host adapters, an MXS824
PCIeswitch, andeBox-basedPCIeexpansionintegration(DolphinInterconnectSolutions
2026b; Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026c; Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026a).
Theprototypesupportsresourcedisaggregationanddevicelending, enablingonenode
to borrow specific PCIe devices attached to another node or to an expansion enclosure
(Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026d). This feature is methodologically important be-
cause it moves evaluation beyond simple point-to-point transfer and into service-like
pooled-resource behavior, which is required for decentralized micro-data center use cases.
Linux-baseddeploymentwasusedasthepracticalimplementationbaselineduetobet-
ter stability and tooling support for the selected PCIe fabric stack. Consumer-grade host
variabilitywasacceptedaspartoftheresearchcontextratherthaneliminatedcompletely,
since one thesis objective is to assess feasibility in realistic non-datacenter hardware en-
vironments.
The evaluation scope in this chapter is therefore divided into:
• Primary scope: validated three-node operational prototype.
• Extended scope: method-compatible expansion to larger node counts and shared
PCIe expansion/device-lending methods.
3.3 Experimental Design and Metrics
The experimental design prioritizes latency and throughput as first-order indicators of
platform usefulness. Metrics are separated into two levels to avoid construct ambiguity:
• Fabric-level metrics: microsecond-scale communication latency and GB/s-scale
transfer throughput measured at the interconnect/resource-pooling layer.
• Service-level metrics: workload completion behavior for mixed household traffic
patternswherepooledresourcesbackpracticaltasks(forexamplecachebackup/sync
and content-serving behavior).
Workload inputs cover a broad data-size range, from small transfers to large payloads,
with tested file sizes spanning approximately 16 MB through 1 GB. The objective is to
11
observe scaling behavior across transfer sizes instead of reporting only a single-point
benchmark.
Baseline comparison is included against both local Ethernet-oriented alternatives and
cloud-oriented service assumptions. Cloud comparison uses representative regional con-
ditions aligned with the Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), Texas operating context to maintain
geographic consistency with expected deployment conditions (Niccum 2026d).
Security controls are included in this chapter as methodological context and light
measurement framing, while full vulnerability detail, attack-path analysis, and mitiga-
tion depth are handled in the dedicated security chapter. Basic encryption and hardening
mechanisms developed during the project are acknowledged where they affect measure-
ment interpretation, but security experimentation is not allowed to dominate Chapter 3’s
performance-centered objective.
Energy and cost signals are collected as supporting indicators rather than as pri-
mary optimization targets. In this stage, software-based estimates are used to character-
ize directional efficiency trends. Composite multi-factor indices (for example, weighted
performance-per-watt-cost scores or single blended utility rankings) are not enforced;
metrics are reported separately unless a directly relevant standard is justified by the
data.
3.4 Data Collection and Analysis Procedure
Data collection proceeded through iterative benchmark and workload runs on the im-
plemented prototype, with logs and output artifacts captured per scenario. Because ex-
periments were conducted during active system development, the procedure emphasizes
pragmatic repeatability over rigid laboratory randomization protocols. Where applicable,
repeated runs were used to verify stability of observed latency/throughput behavior.
Analysis is structured around comparative interpretation:
• intra-system comparison across workload sizes and operating modes,
• cross-baseline comparison against Ethernet and cloud-relevant references,
• interpretationofperformance/securitytradeoffswherehardeningcontrolsarepresent.
The reporting style favors clear, separate metric presentation (latency, throughput,
and supporting operational signals) to preserve interpretability for both research and en-
gineering audiences. Given the thesis phase and available instrumentation, the chapter
avoids over-complicated statistical formalism and instead emphasizes consistency, ob-
served trends, and practical significance in relation to decentralized micro-data center
requirements.
12
3.5 Field-EmbeddedIterationandEngineeringFeed-
back Loops
This research was conducted in a field-embedded mode rather than a sealed laboratory
mode. Practical integration work, benchmark campaigns, and support-oriented trou-
bleshooting informed one another continuously. As a result, method execution included
iterative loops of deploy, diagnose, adjust, and re-measure.
The iterative record documented in project notes (summarized in MySummer) is
used methodologically in this thesis as process evidence, not as a substitute for measured
benchmark data. In practice, this means implementation-era observations can explain
why certain test conditions were chosen or revised, but final claims remain grounded in
instrumented outputs and reproducible procedures.
3.6 Evidence Traceability Model
To preserve claim discipline, each major claim class is mapped to an evidence type:
• Architecture claims map to implemented topology and stack artifacts (Chapter
4).
• Implementation claims map to documented blocker-resolution history (Chapter
5).
• Performanceclaimsmaptobenchmarkdatasetsandstatisticalsummaries(Chap-
ter 6).
• Security claims map to vulnerability analysis and measured mitigation impacts
(Chapter 7).
• Scaling and market claims are labeled as directional unless directly validated
by prototype evidence (Chapters 8-10).
This traceability model is used to separate proven findings from projected pathways
throughout the thesis.
3.7 Validity, Reliability, and Limitations
Internal validity is strengthened by evaluating an implemented platform rather than an
abstract model, and by using direct performance measurements in the same environment
where system features were developed. Reliability is supported through repeated scenario
execution and convergence of results across multiple benchmark perspectives.
13
Several limitations are explicitly acknowledged:
• Hardwareheterogeneity: hostmachinesareconsumersystemswithnon-uniform
capabilities, which introduces variance but also improves real-world relevance.
• Instrumentation constraints: energy analysis relies primarily on software esti-
mates at this stage.
• Experimental control limits: strict randomization/blocking against thermal
drift was not the central organizing strategy during initial campaign runs.
• Security maturity boundary: while the system demonstrates functioning virtu-
alization, pooling, and service hosting capabilities, unresolved security gaps remain
a barrier to immediate commercial-grade deployment.
External validity is moderate: the findings strongly support feasibility and perfor-
mance potential for decentralized residential micro-data centers, but broader commer-
cialization claims require additional hardening, larger field trials, and operational stan-
dardization.
3.8 Reproducibility Protocol
This work adopts a practical reproducibility model suitable for an applied systems thesis.
The goal is to make the workflow reproducible in spirit and structure without requiring
a fully containerized or script-only laboratory stack.
Reproducibility is supported through:
• explicit documentation of topology, node roles, and experimental scope,
• persistent benchmark/output records from the evaluated scenarios,
• clear separation of primary measured metrics (latency and throughput) from sec-
ondary estimates,
• traceablelinkagebetweenmethodologicalsetupinthischapterandempirical/security
findings in later chapters.
This protocol is intentionally medium-granularity: detailed command-level automa-
tion and full parameter manifests are outside the immediate scope of Chapter 3, but
sufficient methodological transparency is provided for readers to reconstruct the core
evaluation process and verify the thesis-level conclusions.
14

Design

4.1 Architecture Scope and Layering
This chapter documents the system architecture in two explicit layers to prevent ambi-
guity between validated engineering results and forward-looking design projections.
The first layer is the implemented prototype architecture, which was physi-
cally deployed, configured, and operated during the benchmark and security campaigns.
Claims in this layer are tied to measurable behavior and operational evidence, and are
intended to support the empirical interpretation in Chapters 5-7 (Niccum 2026a; Niccum
2026c).
The second layer is the proposed scaling architecture, which extends prototype
principles toward neighborhood-scale deployment. This layer captures design intent and
systems trajectory, but it is not treated as fully validated. Where the architecture is
directional rather than proven, assumptions are identified explicitly.
This split also resolves a practical evolution in the project record: early architecture
planning emphasized one idealized topology path, while later implementation converged
on a stable star-style operating configuration with concrete node roles, validated links,
and repeatable diagnostics.
15
4.2 Implemented Prototype Architecture
4.2.1 Hardware Topology and Node Roles
The implemented system was operated as a three-node PCIe fabric testbed with one hub
node and two leaf nodes. In the measured configuration, the hub node (Ghost) served
as the control and observation point for benchmark orchestration and monitoring, while
the two leaf nodes (DolphinBenny1 and DolphinBenny2) acted as remote participants
for transfer, memory, and interrupt-path testing. Both leaf participants were deployed
on off-the-shelf HP OmniDesk desktop systems in the validated baseline environment
(Niccum 2026d).
Operationally, the validated topology behaved as a hub-and-spoke fabric path: each
leaf maintained direct fabric connectivity with the hub, while leaf-to-leaf interaction was
mediated through hub-facing workflows. This structure simplified diagnosis and made
performance comparisons easier to reproduce across runs.
At the role level, the architecture supported three functional responsibilities:
• Coordination role (hub, Ghost): benchmark trigger point, telemetry aggrega-
tion, and operational control.
• Compute/transfer participant role (leaf): remote memory and data-path tar-
get for latency and throughput evaluation.
• Storage/service participant role (leaf): endpoint used in transfer, transparent
access, and service-like access experiments.
This role separation was sufficient for architecture validation without introducing the
complexity of larger multi-hop routing behavior. In a directional extension model, nodes
could be arranged in a daisy-chain pattern where each node also acts as a local hub for
adjacent participants; however, that topology was not the primary validated baseline in
this chapter.
4.2.2 Software Stack and Protocol Layers
The implemented stack followed a layered model:
• Application layer: benchmark programs and monitoring UI components used
to generate measurable workload behavior, including a Java GUI, C-based bench-
mark/testmethods,JSON-structuredpayloadsforpassingmeasurement/statedata,
andJavaScriptwebcomponents. ACloudflareTunnelpathwasalsousedtoprovide
controlled global access to a website hosted on the fabric-backed environment.
16
• Fabric API layer: SISCI primitives for connection, remote segment interac-
tion, synchronization, and transfer operations. In practice, this layer provided
the memory-space integration needed to support shared/combined access behavior
used by the hosted web service workflow.
• Driver/service layer: kernel-level and service-level components responsible for
adapter bring-up, mapping, and runtime control, with Linux Mint used as the
deployment baseline for stable stack operation.
• Hardware layer: PCIe adapters, physical links, and host platform resources that
determine effective bandwidth and latency constraints, including MXH930 host
adapters, an MXS824 switch fabric component, eBox expansion integration, and
the three-node host baseline (Ghost hub plus two HP OmniDesk leaf nodes) (Dol-
phin Interconnect Solutions 2026b; Dolphin Interconnect Solutions 2026c; Dolphin
Interconnect Solutions 2026a; Niccum 2026d).
Two path classes were treated separately during implementation:
• Control path: node discovery, session establishment, and operational orchestra-
tion.
• Data path: payload movement via DMA-oriented or memory-oriented transfer
operations.
The monitoring subsystem (daemon workers plus heartbeat signaling) was part of the
control path, not the bulk-transfer data path. In operational terms, heartbeat intervals
and worker status polling were used to track node liveness and coordination health, while
throughputandlatencymeasurementsweretakenfromtheseparatedata-movementpath.
A key implementation finding was that control-path correctness can coexist with
degraded data-path performance when topology or generation assumptions drift. This
reinforced the need to validate both paths independently.
4.2.3 Memory and Data Path Design
The prototype exercised two complementary memory/data interaction models.
First, explicit transfer paths were used for direct measurement of latency and
throughput behavior. These paths made transport cost visible and were suitable for per-
run statistical analysis. Second, transparent access paths were used to approximate
application-facing semantics where remote resources appear locally accessible through the
stack.
This dual-path approach enabled architectural comparison between raw performance
behavior and usability-oriented abstraction cost. It also made it possible to quantify the
17
penalty (or near-parity) of transparent workflows relative to explicit operations under the
same topology conditions.
At the implementation level, data movement correctness depended on stable link
state, coherent host configuration, and compatible driver/kernel assumptions. When any
of these prerequisites drifted, the architecture could remain partially functional while
producing misleading performance outcomes.
4.2.4 Device Lending and Virtualization Mechanics
Device sharing and virtualization concepts were validated primarily as mechanical ca-
pability rather than as full production orchestration. The prototype demonstrated that
remote-facing resource usage patterns could be presented to applications in a way that
reduces direct awareness of physical placement.
In practice, this behavior depended on:
• consistent node identity and host mapping behavior,
• stable adapter session state,
• predictable topology assumptions,
• and controlled workflow sequencing for add/connect/borrow/return style opera-
tions.
The implementation also showed that virtualization-style convenience does not elimi-
nate low-level dependencies. Topology changes, generation mismatches, or stale configu-
ration artifacts can interrupt lending workflows even when high-level SISCI/eXpressWare
control-interface behavior appears nominal.
4.3 Proposed Scaling Architecture
4.3.1 Extension from Prototype to Neighborhood Topology
The proposed scaling model extends the three-node prototype into a neighborhood-
resident distributed resource fabric. The core architectural principle remains unchanged:
expose pooled storage/compute behavior through high-performance local interconnect
semantics, while minimizing dependence on distant centralized infrastructure for edge-
suitable workloads.
The directional scaling path can be summarized in three steps:
• Pilot mesh scope: limited home-level or lab-level clusters with managed topology
control.
18
• Neighborhood scope: multi-home participation with persistent coordination and
shared service policy.
• Federated scope: inter-neighborhood coordination with stronger routing, trust,
and governance models.
This trajectory is architecturally plausible but not fully validated by the current
prototype. In this thesis, it is treated as structured future design informed by observed
constraints, not as measured deployment fact.
4.3.2 Inter-Home Connectivity and Coordination Assumptions
Neighborhood-scale operation introduces assumptions beyond the validated prototype
boundary:
• Physical inter-home links: stable high-quality connectivity suitable for low-
latency coordination. The future design direction includes a main house computer
connected via PCIe to a router layer that links neighboring homes over PCIe-fiber
paths, with the goal of preserving compatibility across in-home devices while re-
ducing risk from intentional or unintentional consumer-side tampering.
• Persistent always-on coordination nodes: service continuity independent of
end-user workstation power state. Because home routers are generally left powered
on, this layer can provide a more persistent coordination anchor and temporary
memory-state continuity when a resident powers down their primary computer.
• Identity, trust, and authorization models: stronger control of segment access
and resource borrowing. In the current state, this area still requires substantial
security upgrades, which are addressed in the dedicated security chapter.
• Operational governance: shared policies for ownership, scheduling, and con-
tention resolution. Directionally, these governance controls can be built on top of
existing SISCI capabilities rather than requiring a full control-plane redesign from
scratch.
• Security hardening maturity: closure of unresolved high-severity gaps identified
in Chapter 7.
Until these assumptions are implemented and measured, neighborhood architecture
claims remain projected pathways.
19
4.4 Design Tradeoffs and Constraints
Implementation and architecture analysis revealed several non-trivial tradeoffs.
Topology simplicity versus scale realism: hub-oriented topology improved re-
peatability and diagnosis quality, but does not fully represent larger decentralized traffic
patterns. House-to-housecapabilityisdemonstratedatprototypescope,whileneighborhood-
scale organization still requires additional coordination design, validation, and field test-
ing.
Transparency versus diagnosability: transparent access abstractions improve us-
ability, but can obscure where performance or correctness failures originate unless explicit
diagnostics are preserved. In a layered system, application software, middleware, API be-
havior, and low-level transport/hardware state all interact, which can make root-cause
attribution ambiguous without path-specific instrumentation.
Hardware capability versus effective path capability: end-device generation
specifications are insufficient predictors of realized throughput when intermediate switch-
ing or topology constraints reduce effective link behavior. Geographic scaling, especially
in early deployment phases, will likely depend on existing infrastructure segments that
can introduce upstream bottlenecks beyond local adapter capability.
Heterogeneity tolerance versus stability: consumer-grade host diversity im-
provesreal-worldrelevancebutincreasesintegrationeffort,particularlyaroundkernel/driver
compatibility and lifecycle management. In practice, SISCI stack stability is coupled to
kernel version changes, so host updates can require coordinated driver and software main-
tenance.
Rapid iteration versus strict experimental control: active implementation im-
proved systems maturity quickly by allowing fast diagnose-fix-retest cycles, but this speed
introduces interpretive risk because not all variables remain fixed between runs. As a re-
sult, results must be interpreted with strict configuration tracking so improvements are
not incorrectly attributed to a single change when multiple stack elements evolved to-
gether.
These constraints are not incidental; they define the architectural maturity boundary
that separates present feasibility from deployment-grade reliability.

Table 4.1 summarizes the boundary used throughout the remainder of the thesis.
This boundary table is normative for later chapters: Chapter 6 evaluates implemented
performance behavior, Chapter 7 evaluates current security posture, and Chapter 10
discusses projected scaling only within clearly marked future-work constraints.

5.1 Implementation Context and Source Basis
This chapter documents the implementation phase that translated the architecture in
Chapter 4 into operational systems. The narrative is grounded in deployment records,
benchmark campaign notes, troubleshooting logs, and the consolidated implementation
summary in MySummer (Niccum 2026c). Its purpose is to provide traceable engineering
context for the measured outcomes reported in Chapter 6 and the risk posture discussed
in Chapter 7.
The chapter is intentionally practice-embedded. It does not treat implementation as
a clean linear build, but as an iterative sequence of deployment, diagnosis, reconfigura-
tion, and validation under realistic hardware and operational constraints. To preserve
confidentiality and research ethics, customer-identifiable details and sensitive operational
artifacts are excluded. The emphasis remains on transferable technical patterns: what
failed, how failure was isolated, what changed, and which verification criteria confirmed
recovery.
22
5.2 Phase 1: Initial Bring-Up and Installer Valida-
tion
The first implementation phase focused on basic remote operability and installation cor-
rectness across the target nodes. Initial progress included SSH access, OS and kernel
identification, installer staging via secure copy, and firmware update/reset workflows.
Early diagnostics revealed a procedural gap: installation artifacts had been transferred
but not actually executed on all nodes. This was corrected through explicit permission
setting and controlled installer execution, followed by firmware checks, adapter resets,
and reboot-based state revalidation.
Thekeyoutputofthisphasewasarepeatablebring-upsequencethatreducedambigu-
ity during later fault isolation. Rather than treating installation as a one-time event, the
workflow was standardized as a loop: transfer, execute, verify driver and firmware state,
reset if required, reboot, and re-check adapter/session visibility. This procedural baseline
became the control path for subsequent compatibility and performance debugging.
5.3 Phase 2: Link Health and Physical-Layer Trou-
bleshooting
After basic bring-up, link-state warnings emerged, most notably degraded lane width (x8
where x16 was expected). Software-side configuration attempts alone did not clear the
warnings, and repeated logical reconfiguration produced no stable improvement. At this
point the investigation shifted from software tuning to cross-layer diagnosis.
Built-intoolingwascentralduringthisphase. dis_diag wasusedtoverifyadapter/session
health and link-state anomalies, dis_config to inspect runtime topology and partition
behavior, and dis_mkconf to regenerate expected configuration state after topology cor-
rections. Thedishosts.conf host-mappingfilewasalsotreatedasafirst-classdiagnostic
artifact to confirm node identity consistency during recovery.
The decisive finding in this phase was physical-layer: cable integrity and attachment
state were inconsistent with expected topology. Once corrected, adapter reset and re-
boot cycles restored the intended x16 operating state and active partition behavior. This
phase established an important implementation principle used throughout the project:
PCIe fabric anomalies must be treated as coupled hardware-software problems, not as in-
dependent software defects. In practical terms, no configuration-level claim was accepted
until both diagnostic output and physical topology checks converged.
23
5.4 Phase 3: OS and Kernel Alignment Under Real
Constraints
With link health recovered, the dominant instability source shifted to OS and kernel com-
patibility drift between nodes. Multiple installation and recovery cycles were required to
align systems on mutually compatible kernel families and driver expectations. Attempts
to resolve drift through package-level changes alone were insufficient in several cases,
leading to local-console recovery, boot-media reinstall paths, and BIOS-level escalation.
An explicit platform comparison emerged in this phase. Both Windows and Linux
were technically available paths for SISCI-based operation, but Linux produced more
stable outcomes in the implemented environment, particularly around predictable bus-
address ordering during boot and subsequent service bring-up behavior. In contrast, plat-
formvariationinearlyWindowsattemptsincreasedoperationalfrictionduringadapter/service
initialization, so Linux was adopted as the practical baseline for repeatable execution.
This phase also exposed a lifecycle risk in Linux environments: unattended or auto-
matic system updates can change kernel versions, which can in turn disable or invalidate
currently working SISCI service bindings until matching components are reinstalled or
revalidated. For this reason, stable and intentionally controlled kernel baselines were pre-
ferred over continuously changing update tracks for benchmark and integration phases.
Relatedtothis,DolphinprovidesmultipleSISCI/eXpressWarereleasevariantsaligned
to specific OS families and kernel ranges. Deployment reliability depended on selecting
the correct stack version for the exact platform state, rather than assuming one installer
path would remain valid across kernel transitions.
This phase revealed that repeated installer failure can be a secondary symptom rather
than a root cause. In the observed cases, kernel and firmware interactions were often the
primary blockers, while installer behavior reflected downstream incompatibility. Stabi-
lization required harmonizing node baselines before higher-level service assumptions (for
example host mapping and service orchestration) could be trusted. The result was a more
reliable compatibility model for future deployments: align platform baselines first, then
evaluate stack-level behavior.
5.5 Phase 4: Performance Validation and Switch In-
tegration
Once baseline stability was established, the implementation focus moved to benchmark-
informed validation. Diagnostic criteria included clean topology visibility, valid session
status across nodes, and warning/error-free adapter health outputs. Performance tools
24
were then used to characterize throughput and latency behavior across multiple perspec-
tives.
Built-in test utilities were central to this phase, including dma_bench for DMA-
oriented throughput characterization and scimemcpy for latency-oriented measurement
under PIO-style memory-copy paths. Direct Memory Access (DMA) represents bulk
transfer behavior where data movement is offloaded from continuous CPU handling, mak-
ing it suitable for sustained throughput evaluation. Programmed I/O (PIO) represents
CPU-mediated copy behavior, which is more sensitive to per-operation overhead and is
therefore useful for fine-grained latency observation. Together, these tools provided a
consistent low-level baseline before higher-level application benchmarks were interpreted.
Switch integration introduced a second-order systems effect: link behavior was con-
strained by the least capable component in the path. In practice, Gen4-capable adapters
routed through a Gen3 switch exhibited effective throttling relative to direct-link expec-
tations. This mismatch produced recurring operational noise until host configuration ex-
pectations were regenerated to match the effective fabric path. The engineering outcome
was procedural: every topology change must be followed by configuration regeneration,
log reset, and post-change verification, otherwise stale assumptions can masquerade as
runtime defects.
This phase also included building a personal catalog of known-good cluster layouts
and configuration combinations for future reference. Maintaining this catalog reduced
repeated trial-and-error during later setup work and provided a practical baseline for
bringing new clusters online more efficiently.
This phase also reinforced the interpretation boundary used in Chapter 6: benchmark
values represent measured behavior under concrete topology conditions and should not
be generalized across unvalidated hardware paths.
5.6 Phase5: SupportEngineeringandTechnicalCom-
munication
As system understanding matured, implementation work expanded from local diagnostics
to support-facing technical communication. The same deployment lessons used internally
were translated into structured customer guidance covering installation prerequisites,
host identification constraints, configuration propagation behavior, and cluster formation
dependencies.
A significant improvement in this phase was diagnostic minimization. Instead of
requesting broad data dumps, support exchanges were structured around minimum suf-
ficient evidence first (for example host mapping files and primary diagnostic outputs),
then expanded only when ambiguity remained. This reduced cycle time, improved repro-
25
ducibility, and made troubleshooting recommendations easier to validate.
The phase demonstrates that implementation quality in distributed infrastructure is
not only a function of code and hardware, but also of communication precision. Oper-
ational clarity became a technical asset: better requests produced better evidence, and
better evidence produced faster resolution.
5.7 Phase6: SISCIApplicationPrototypingandDemo
Evolution
In parallel with platform stabilization, prototype application work was used to test
whether infrastructure capabilities were practically consumable at the software layer.
The most explicit example was a two-node SISCI "vanishing text" chat concept designed
around shared-memory primitives: a presence heartbeat segment and an append-only
event ring with sequence and expiration semantics.
AnadditionalpracticalobservationfromthisphasewasthatDolphinhardwarebehav-
ior is, in many cases, largely transparent to applications that are not explicitly designed
to call SISCI primitives. This transparency is useful for compatibility, but SISCI-aware
application design is still required when software must directly control remote segment
behavior, synchronization semantics, or fabric-specific resource workflows.
This effort provided two implementation benefits. First, it forced explicit think-
ing about application-visible consistency, event ordering, and time-to-live behavior un-
der distributed memory exchange. Second, it exposed practical adaptation constraints
when moving from earlier three-node assumptions to stable two-node operational modes.
Complementary demo workflows (including SmartIO device-lending procedures for cap-
ture/borrow/return paths) further linked low-level fabric behavior to user-facing appli-
cation scenarios.
The result was not a production application, but a validated bridge from infrastruc-
ture mechanics to software design patterns, which supports the systems-to-application
argument developed in Chapters 4 and 10.
5.8 Debugging and Resolution Patterns
Across all phases, several recurring debugging patterns emerged:
• Symptom isolation before optimization. Performance tuning was deferred
until baseline health, topology visibility, and version compatibility were confirmed.
• Cross-layer verification. Software diagnostics were always paired with physical
and topology checks when anomalies persisted.
26
• Configuration drift control. Topology or hardware changes were treated as
configuration events requiring explicit regeneration and revalidation.
• Repeatable verification loops. Recovery actions were considered complete only
after deterministic re-checks across diagnostics, sessions, and expected operating
state.
• Evidence-first communication. Internal and external troubleshooting both im-
proved when requests were anchored to minimum sufficient artifacts.
A personal practice reinforced this pattern: before escalating for support, I tried
to solve every component of the issue that was independently testable, so the remaining
unknowns more clearly identified the likely root cause. This approach was first formalized
in my CSE 1320 coursework and has remained a consistent part of my troubleshooting
method throughout my collegiate work.
These patterns reduced rework and created a practical template for future deploy-
ments where perfect hardware uniformity cannot be assumed.
5.9 Operational Lessons for Deployment-Grade Sys-
tems
This implementation journey supports five deployment-grade lessons.
First, installation success is necessary but not sufficient; stable operation depends on
synchronized platform baselines and explicit compatibility management. Second, PCIe
fabric reliability is inherently cross-layer, and diagnosis must account for hardware path,
firmware state, and software configuration together. Third, measured performance is
topology-bound and must be interpreted with path-specific context. Fourth, support
engineering practices materially affect technical outcomes by shaping evidence quality
and turnaround time. Fifth, application prototyping is a useful systems test because it
exposes assumptions that synthetic benchmarks can miss.
Theselessonsbridgedirectlyintolaterchapters. Chapter6quantifiestheperformance
behavior that remained after these implementation controls were applied. Chapter 7
evaluates the security posture of the resulting system and distinguishes implemented
mitigations from deferred controls. Chapter 10 then uses the implementation evidence to
separate validated findings from projected commercialization pathways.

6.1 Evaluation Objectives
This chapter evaluates the implemented three-node PCIe fabric system under controlled
benchmark conditions and answers three bounded questions:
1. RDMAPIOreadlatency(RemoteMemoryDemo): mean1.724µsacrossruns,
with p99 fixed at 2.000 µs in repeated 1,000-iteration sequences, indicating tightly
bounded remote read behavior under the tested conditions.
2. Transparent memory cycle latency (Transparency Demo): mean 1.978 µs for
write+flush+read cycles, showing only a modest added cost relative to explicit remote
reads while preserving transparent-access semantics.
3. Interrupt round-trip latency (Interrupt Demo): steady-state mean 30.688 µs,
with a best-case floor near 20 µs but run-level p99 in the high-hundreds of microsec-
onds, highlighting scheduler-sensitive tail behavior despite stable central tendency.
The objective is not to prove full neighborhood-scale deployment performance. In-
stead, the chapter provides evidence for the currently implemented architecture and es-
tablishes the performance baseline used by the synthesis chapters (Niccum 2026d).
28
6.2 Benchmark Environment
Benchmarks were run on the implemented three-node star-style topology described in
Chapters 4 and 5. One node acted as the benchmark controller and hub, with two leaf
nodes connected via dual x4 links. Measured traffic in this chapter focuses on direct
hub-to-leaf paths.
The software stack used Dolphin SISCI services and benchmark applications targeting
four quantitative domains:
• DMA bulk transfer throughput,
• remote memory PIO read latency,
• transparent memory write-flush-read cycle cost,
• interrupt round-trip signaling latency.
Each benchmark was repeated across multiple runs (minimum five runs for the quanti-
tative summary sets), with microsecond-precision timing and structured output capture.
A practical operations background load was maintained through active metrics agents,
reflecting realistic rather than fully synthetic idle-lab conditions.
6.3 Measured Results
6.3.1 Latency Results
Latency measurements were captured for three operation classes:
• RDMA PIO read latency (Remote Memory Demo): mean 1.724 µs across
runs, with consistent p99 of 2.000 µs across 1,000-iteration sequences.
• Transparent memory cycle latency (Transparency Demo): mean 1.978 µs
for write+flush+read cycles.
• Interrupt round-trip latency (Interrupt Demo): steady-state mean 30.688
µs, with best-case floor near 20 µs and run-level p99 values in the high-hundreds of
microseconds.

6.3.2 Throughput Results
Throughput was measured through DMA transfer benchmarks using 64 MB and 128

These values represent effective per-path behavior in the validated topology and are

upgrade on the hub node.

6.3.3 Extended Throughput Observations from Norway Clus-
ters
In additional full-width x16 cluster measurements conducted in the Norway office, sus-
tained throughput was consistently observed around 25 GB/s on PCIe Gen4 systems and
around 42 GB/s on PCIe Gen5 systems. In the same environment, the best recorded
Gen5 throughput exceeded 50 GB/s.
For the measured Gen5 cluster used in this study context, the limiting factor was
node memory-path quality rather than interconnect capacity, indicating that the PCIe
fabric itself was not the dominant bottleneck at the achieved rates. The lowest observed
PIO data-transfer latency in the Norway measurements was 0.540 µs.
These Norway results are included as practical field evidence from higher-width plat-
forms and should be interpreted as complementary to, rather than directly interchange-
able with, the three-node hub-and-leaf benchmark set summarized above.
30
6.3.4 Overhead and Stability Results
Measured overhead and stability behavior include:
• DMA CPU overhead: during active Linux data transfers, CPU usage was main-
tained under 2%; DMA payload movement is hardware-offloaded and does not
consume CPU for the transfer path itself.
• RDMA consistency: low run-to-run deviation for average PIO read latency, with
stable p99 at 2.000 µs in the recorded run set.
• Transparent-access overhead delta: transparent write-flush-read cycles re-
mained close to explicit read latency scale, with measurable but modest additional
cycle cost.
• Interrupt tail behavior: average signaling latency remained in the tens of mi-
croseconds while tail latency reflected scheduler and dispatch variability, because
interrupt handling traverses kernel wakeup and thread-dispatch paths rather than
direct memory-read hardware paths.
Across the quantitative benchmark campaign used for summary reporting, completion
success remained high with no structural collapse of the measurement pipeline.
6.4 Interpretation and Tradeoff Analysis
The measured results indicate a clear operational separation between data movement and
signaling costs.
First, DMA paths provide high sustained throughput with low CPU burden, sup-
porting resource-pooling patterns where large payload movement dominates. Second,
explicit RDMA reads provide microsecond-scale access suitable for latency-sensitive con-
trol and metadata interaction. Third, transparent memory access offers a development-
productivity tradeoff: a small additional cycle cost in exchange for simpler programming
semantics.
Interrupt signaling behaves differently from memory-read paths. The mean round-
trip signaling latency is substantially higher than PIO read latency, which is expected
because interrupt workflows traverse kernel wakeup and dispatch paths. This makes
interrupts appropriate for event-driven synchronization, but less suitable as a substitute
for fine-grained polling-free data fetch in ultra-tight latency loops.
At a systems level, the benchmark set supports a mixed strategy:
• use DMA for payload transfer,
• use RDMA-style reads for fast state access,
31
• use interrupts for control-plane event notification.
6.5 Interpretation Against Workload Expectations
Fordecentralizedneighborhoodinfrastructuregoals, thecurrentresultssupportfeasibility
in the following workload classes:
• high-rate local data synchronization,
• low-latency distributed metadata/state exchange,
• mixed control-and-payload service pipelines where compute and storage placement
are disaggregated.
The measurements also clarify where caution is required. The validated topology is
limited in node count and routing complexity, so these values should be interpreted as
prototype-scope behavior rather than direct proof of multi-neighborhood or internet-scale
operation. In other words, the results are strong evidence of local fabric capability, not
full market-scale deployment performance.
6.6 Measurement Caveats and Experimental Bound-
aries
Several boundaries shaped this measurement campaign:
• Topology boundary: star-style hub-and-leaf operation was the validated mode;
direct leaf-to-leaf performance was not the primary measured path.
• Node-count boundary: the campaign reflects three-node behavior, not large-
cluster contention dynamics.
• Live-development context: measurements were collected after substantial sta-
bilization work but still within an active engineering environment.
• Hardware-path dependency: effective behavior depended on actual link path
characteristics, including generation constraints in switch-mediated paths.
• Scheduler sensitivity: interrupt-tail behavior was influenced by OS dispatch
dynamics and thread wake timing.
These caveats do not invalidate the benchmark results; they define how far those
results should be generalized.
32
6.7 Performance Limitations
The observed limitations fall into two categories.
Fundamental platform-linked limits:
• per-path throughput bounded by effective link characteristics (for example negoti-
ated lane width, PCIe generation, switch-path quality, and NUMA/memory-path
behavior on participating nodes),
• interrupt signaling cost bounded by kernel-mediated notification flow; in this work,
Linux provided the most consistent low-latency behavior, while fastest response
generallydependsonlow-latency/preempt-orientedkernelconfigurationandsystem
tuning rather than a single universally best kernel version,
• topology-induced concentration effects in hub-routed traffic; a future daisy-chain
operating rule can reduce single-hub concentration by having each node act as a
hub for its two adjacent neighbors.
Current implementation limits:
• configuration sensitivity after topology changes,
• limited validated node scale,
• incomplete characterization of mixed multi-flow contention in larger operational
meshes.
Taken together, the benchmark evidence supports a strong prototype-scale perfor-
mance claim: the implemented architecture delivers low-latency memory interaction and
high-throughput DMA behavior suitable for localized decentralized infrastructure pat-
terns. Broader scaling claims remain conditional on future validation under expanded
topology, security hardening, and operational governance constraints.
33

7.1 Threat Model and Assumptions
Security analysis in this thesis is anchored to a residential or community-shared deploy-
ment context rather than a single-tenant datacenter context. The key shift is environ-
mental: nodes that participate in the PCIe fabric are also internet-exposed household
systems, and operator trust is distributed rather than centralized (Niccum 2026f).
The threat model assumes that at least one node may be compromised through con-
ventional endpoint vectors, physical access to portions of interconnect infrastructure may
be possible, insider behavior across fabric members cannot be treated as universally
trusted, and security controls must coexist with strict performance requirements.
Trust boundaries are therefore drawn at three levels: (1) between local host mem-
ory and DMA-capable fabric devices, (2) between fabric nodes sharing SISCI-accessible
segments, and (3) between internet-facing processes and fabric control/data planes.
7.2 Attack Surface Characterization
The evaluated attack surface includes seven operationally meaningful classes:
34
DMA memory exposure. Incomplete or absent IOMMU (Input-Output Memory
Management Unit) enforcement can permit unsafe physical-memory reach from DMA-
capable devices. The IOMMU is the hardware/firmware protection layer that constrains
which memory ranges a device is allowed to access. In a shared fabric, weak enforcement
raises the risk that compromise at one endpoint can be transformed into unauthorized
memory interaction on another host.
Credential-free remote segment access. Segment connection semantics based
primarily on node ID and segment ID provide weak identity assurance when stronger
authentication is not present. This creates a path where knowledge of addressing con-
ventions may be sufficient to attempt unauthorized cross-node access.
Internet-to-fabric pivot paths. Internet-facing services on participant nodes cre-
ate a practical pivot risk: a conventional endpoint compromise can be escalated into
fabric-level abuse. The consequence is that external attack surface and interconnect
trust boundaries are tightly coupled.
Plaintext interconnect traffic. Without encryption safeguards, memory and data
movement across physical links may be observable to actors with link-level or device-
adjacent access. This exposes confidentiality risk for sensitive payloads, metadata, or
control signaling.
No effective rate control. Absent robust transfer and interrupt rate limiting,
denial-of-service behavior can be induced through flooding patterns. Even when confi-
dentiality is unaffected, uncontrolled bursts can degrade fairness and inflate latency for
legitimate workloads.
Configuration integrity weakness. Trusted topology and control files become a
high-leveragetargetwhenintegritycontrolsareweakorinconsistent. Tamperingcanalter
trust relationships, routing assumptions, or enforcement behavior without immediately
obvious operational failure.
Limiteddefaultobservability. InsufficientaudittraceattheSISCI/controlbound-
ary constrains post-incident reconstruction and attribution. In practice, this makes it
harder to distinguish benign misconfiguration from adversarial manipulation during in-
cident response.
Together, these attack surfaces show that high-performance interconnect assumptions
that are acceptable in tightly controlled HPC environments do not transfer directly to
shared residential deployments.
7.3 Vulnerability Findings
Seven vulnerabilities were identified and prioritized by severity:
• V-1 (Critical): incomplete IOMMU protection enables unsafe DMA exposure.
35
• V-2 (Critical): credential-free cross-node segment accessibility.
• V-3 (High): insufficient isolation boundaries between endpoint compromise and
fabric control paths.
• V-4 (High): unencrypted PCIe fabric traffic.
• V-5 (Medium): no robust transfer/interrupt rate limiting for abuse scenarios.
• V-6 (Medium): no dependable integrity enforcement for key fabric configuration
files in baseline mode.
• V-7 (Medium): no default SISCI operation audit trail at the needed granularity.
The most consequential architectural finding is that two vulnerabilities remained on
the critical path after the implementation sprint: authenticated segment access (V-2)
and fabric traffic confidentiality (V-4). These are not incremental tuning issues; they are
deployment-blocking items for shared-production contexts.
7.4 Mitigation Design and Implementation
Five mitigation tracks were executed or attempted during the implementation sprint,
with outcomes separated below.
Implemented/partial controls with measured outputs:
• Fix 1: IOMMU strict-mode enforcement (V-1) – Partial. Applied across
nodes; leaf-node isolation improved, while hub-node platform limits prevented uni-
form full isolation. Measured impact: DMA throughput from 14.326 GB/s to 14.18
GB/s (about -1.0%), and RDMA latency from 1.724 µs to 1.80 µs (about +4.4%).
• Fix3: isolationhardening(V-3)–Partial/applicability-bounded. Network-
namespace isolation was not applicable on the evaluated NTB exposure model
(no fabric Network Interface Card (NIC) exposed in the standard IP stack), but
AppArmor-based /dev/SISCI access restriction was implemented and verified on
the active metrics path.
• Fix 4: DMA/interrupt rate limiting (V-5) – Partial. Token-bucket control
successfully capped attacker DMA throughput (13.310 GB/s to 8.396 GB/s), but
didnotmateriallyimprovevictimPIOlatencyatthetestedcap,indicatingqueueing
contention remained significant.
• Fix 5: extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) audit logging (V-7) –
Success. Tracepoint-based filtering was implemented at the kernel-event level and
36
scoped to the SISCI device major so that only relevant ioctl calls were recorded
while unrelated system-call traffic was ignored. This selective capture improved
audit visibility without broad tracing overhead; measured impact remained mini-
mal (DMA throughput delta about -0.07%, RDMA latency unchanged in reported
baseline).
Attempted but not production-viable in current environment:
• Fix 2: IMA-based config integrity enforcement (V-6) – Failed in current
distro/kernel operational mode. Repeated low-level enforcement failures ef-
fectively bricked the system several times, requiring full recovery cycles including
Linux reinstallation, SISCI stack reinstallation, and redevelopment-environment re-
builds (including IDE tooling), and ultimately led to abandoning this approach for
the current build context.
Deferred high-severity controls:
• Authenticated capability-token segment control (V-2).
• Fabric encryption strategy (V-4), including software and hardware-path op-
tions.
Theimplementationoutcomeisthereforebestdescribedasriskreductionwithbounded
maturity, not full closure.
7.5 Security-Performance Tradeoffs
Measured security-performance tradeoffs were mixed but informative.
IOMMU strict-mode hardening introduced measurable but moderate overhead, with
approximately1%throughputreductionandlow-single-digitmicrosecondlatencyincrease
in the benchmark context. eBPF audit instrumentation imposed near-negligible through-
put cost at the measured scale. By contrast, rate limiting meaningfully constrained
attacker-side bandwidth but did not, at the tested policy threshold, restore victim-side
latency to baseline.
The main tradeoff pattern is therefore not "security always reduces performance."
Instead, it is control-specific:
• memory isolation controls add small steady overhead,
• observability controls can be low-cost when designed at tracepoint granularity,
• abuse-prevention controls require policy tuning to improve fairness, not only at-
tacker suppression.
37
Unknowns remain for deferred controls, especially authenticated segment gating and
full traffic confidentiality, where overhead was not yet characterized empirically in this
environment.
7.6 Operational Risk Bridge from Field Implemen-
tation
Implementation evidence from Chapter 5 materially shaped the security interpretation
in this chapter.
First, configuration drift and topology changes repeatedly produced states where sys-
tems remained partially functional but semantically unsafe or misleading. From a se-
curity perspective, this is critical: silent drift can mask weakened control assumptions.
Second, access-path dependencies (for example service startup ordering, host-mapping
correctness, and node identity consistency) directly affected trust decisions and enforce-
ment reliability. Third, operational recovery pressure can encourage bypass behavior if
hardening mechanisms are brittle, as demonstrated by the practical infeasibility of one
integrity-enforcement path in the active environment.
The operational lesson is that security control design must include deployment re-
silience criteria. Controls that are theoretically strong but operationally fragile will be
disabled, bypassed, or postponed in real deployments, preserving structural risk.
7.7 Residual Risk and Hardening Roadmap
Residual risk remains above deployment-grade threshold for shared residential commer-
cialization. The most important unresolved items are V-2 and V-4, both high-impact
and both architecture-level concerns.
A prioritized hardening roadmap is:
1. Implementauthenticatedsegment-accesscontrol(capability/tokenmodel)with
explicit expiry, revocation, and audit linkage.
2. Add fabric confidentiality controls appropriate to hardware/software constraints,
then benchmark overhead under representative load.
3. Rework configuration integrity strategy to a deployment-safe mechanism com-
patible with the operating environment.
4. Tune abuse controls (rate limits, queue fairness) based on victim-side latency tar-
gets, not attacker bandwidth alone.
38
5. Expand policy-hardening coverage from pilot binaries to the full service surface
(startup scripts, service units, control utilities, and user-facing processes), using staged
enforcement that progresses from audit-only mode to selective blocking and then full
enforcement after stability validation.
In summary, the prototype is security-improved but not security-complete. It is suit-
ableforcontrolledresearchanditerativehardening, butnotyetsuitableforunconstrained
multi-tenant neighborhood deployment without the deferred controls and additional val-
idation.
39

8.2 NVIDIA/SPAN Technical Claims
SPAN’s whitepaper frames XFRA as a distributed compute cloud built from residential
and small-business Nodes that combine GPU modules, panel-level power control, battery-
backed resilience, and fleet orchestration via XSOL (Span Team 2026b). The stated value
proposition is rapid, incremental AI-inference capacity growth under grid constraints,
with latency-aware workload placement and failover during power events rather than a
replacement of hyperscale training data centers (Span Team 2026b). NVIDIA appears
in this context as an initial launch partner aligned to the compute hardware and deploy-
ment narrative, while SPAN positions itself as the power-orchestration and distributed-
operations layer (Span Team 2026a; Span Team 2026b).
These claims are strategically significant for this thesis because they validate the rele-
vance of edge-local resource coordination while highlighting a different systems emphasis.
The thesis evidence is grounded in low-level interconnect behavior and measured secu-
rity/performance tradeoffs, whereas XFRA public material foregrounds power-aware fleet
operations, deployment velocity, and market-facing scale pathways (Span Team 2026b).
8.3 Comparative Framework
8.3.1 Architecture and Topology
The thesis architecture is prototype-centered and explicit about node roles, topology
boundaries, and control/data separation in a PCIe-fabric setting. SPAN’s XFRA archi-
tecture is also explicit, but at a different layer: residential/small-business Nodes, SPAN
panel telemetry/control, local energy storage, and XSOL coordination over a low-latency
network fabric with power-event failover behavior (Span Team 2026b). Both approaches
treat edge-local infrastructure as a coordinated system rather than isolated endpoints,
but they optimize different bottlenecks. This thesis primarily addresses infrastructure-
path determinism and measured behavior; XFRA primarily addresses power-constrained
capacity deployment and fleet orchestration.
8.3.2 Data Movement and Virtualization Model
The thesis focuses on high-performance resource interaction through PCIe-fabric seman-
tics, including segment operations and device-lending behavior, which provides strong lo-
calitycharacteristicsanddirectcontrolofdata-pathassumptions. XFRAinsteadpresents
workload mobility across many independent Nodes, where scheduling is informed by la-
tency targets, Node health, and real-time site power constraints (Span Team 2026b). In
effect, the thesis prioritizes deterministic substrate behavior while XFRA prioritizes geo-
42
graphically distributed dispatch and energy-aware orchestration. The two models are not
mutually exclusive: substrate-level efficiency and fleet-level orchestration can be layered
together in future systems.
8.3.3 Trust, Security, and Privacy Model
The thesis security model is explicit and adversarial for shared residential settings: vul-
nerabilities are enumerated, mitigations are implemented and tested, and unresolved con-
trols are clearly marked. XFRA public material presents a concrete control posture at
claim level, including encrypted communications, identity/access controls, multi-tenant
workload isolation, audit logging, tamper-evident protections, and credential revocation
paths (Span Team 2026b). Convergence exists in objective (secure local infrastructure),
while divergence remains in evidence form: this thesis emphasizes measured findings and
failure boundaries, while XFRA materials emphasize designed controls and staged rollout
confidence.
8.3.4 Deployment and Economics
Fromadeploymentstandpoint,thethesisshowsthattechnicalviabilitydoesnotautomat-
ically produce operational simplicity; configuration discipline, troubleshooting maturity,
and environment-specific hardening are decisive. XFRA’s model addresses this challenge
by standardizing a repeatable Node package and claiming incremental rollout through
existing behind-the-meter capacity, beginning with pilot phases and expanding toward
larger U.S. deployment targets in 2027 (Span Team 2026b). From an economics stand-
point, both directions depend on utilization and operations quality, but XFRA more
explicitly centers utility-grid constraints, homeowner incentives, and capacity time-to-
market as primary economic levers (Span Team 2026a; Span Team 2026b).
8.4 Convergence, Divergence, andStrategic Implica-
tions
Thecentralstrategicimplicationisthatthisthesisisneitherinvalidatednorcompletedby
industry convergence; instead, convergence increases relevance while raising the quality
bar for validation. Convergence is clear in the shared recognition that distributed, edge-
local infrastructure can address latency, locality, and deployment-speed pressures. Diver-
gence is equally clear in execution style: this thesis is prototype-bound, measurement-
heavy, and security-gated, while SPAN/XFRA is platform-broad, power-orchestration-
heavy, and market-forward in deployment ambition (Span Team 2026b). The practical
43
strategy is therefore to continue rigorous infrastructure validation while preparing inte-
gration interfaces to broader orchestration ecosystems that are likely to shape commercial
adoption.
8.5 Positioning of This Thesis in the New Industry
Context
In the current context, this thesis is best positioned as an evidence-backed infrastructure
study that complements broader platform narratives rather than competing with them
on marketing scope. Its durable value is the combination of concrete implementation
records, measured performance/security tradeoff evidence, and disciplined boundaries
between what is proven and what remains projected. That positioning supports both
academic and applied outcomes: it offers publishable technical depth while providing
an actionable engineering base for future integration with larger distributed-compute
ecosystems (Span Team 2026b).
44
