9.1 Role Transition: Researcher to Industry Engi-
neer
The work trajectory evolved from hypothesis framing into hands-on systems engineer-
ing. Early project phases emphasized architecture concepts and benchmark planning.
As implementation progressed, responsibilities shifted toward deployment support, fault
isolation, environment bring-up, and repeatability validation (Niccum 2026c).
This role transition materially improved the thesis quality in two ways. First, it
exposed assumptions that were plausible in design form but fragile in operational real-
ity. Second, it generated a disciplined loop between measurement and troubleshooting,
allowing claims to be anchored in behavior observed under real integration pressure.
One practical anecdote illustrates this plausibility gap: the earliest concept draft
centered on Raspberry Pi nodes and did not yet include a PCIe-fabric core. Before pro-
posal submission, Dolphin feedback redirected that path toward PCIe-based architecture,
whichultimatelymadethethesisbothmoretechnicallydemandingandmorealignedwith
high-performance infrastructure realities.
45
9.2 Training and Field Exposure
Field exposure included installation workflows, configuration handling, diagnostics pro-
cedures, and troubleshooting of vendor-stack interaction points. These activities changed
several original assumptions:
• setup complexity was higher than initial conceptual framing suggested,
• configuration integrity and startup sequencing were more critical than expected,
• and support tooling literacy (logs, low-level checks, benchmark interpretation) was
essential for progress.
A substantial part of this exposure came through a three-week training period in
Norway, working directly at the operational location as part of the implementation-
learning phase.
Thepracticalimplicationisthatsystemsfeasibilityisjointlytechnicalandprocedural.
A design can be logically correct yet operationally unreliable without adequate field-
informed process discipline.
9.3 Engineering and Productization Insights
Several transferable lessons emerged.
Installationreality. Documentationquality, dependencyordering, andenvironment
parity repeatedly proved to be first-order delivery risks rather than secondary implemen-
tation details. In practice, many blocked states were not caused by core architecture
flaws, but by sequencing mismatches, version assumptions, or host-environment diver-
gence during bring-up.
Diagnostics cadence. Rapid hypothesis-test loops consistently reduced downtime
and limited speculative rework. Short, structured debugging cycles (test, observe, iso-
late, retest) were more effective than broad one-shot changes, especially when multiple
potential failure points existed across drivers, services, and fabric configuration.
Configuration discipline. Small file-level drift produced disproportionately large
behavioral ambiguity in distributed setups. A minor mismatch in identifiers, mapping
files, or startup parameters could mimic deeper system instability, so strict configuration
tracking and repeatable baselining became essential to distinguish true platform limita-
tions from avoidable operational error.
Benchmark literacy. Raw throughput values alone were not enough for credible
interpretation. Practical evaluation required reading throughput together with queueing
behavior, contention dynamics, and fairness outcomes, so that "fast" results were not
46
misread when latency tails, victim impact, or scheduler effects were the actual limiting
factors.
These lessons are relevant beyond this stack. Any emerging decentralized infrastruc-
tureeffortwilllikelyfacesimilartranslationchallengesfromprototypedemostosustained
operations.
9.4 What Changed in the Original Assumptions
Proposal-era assumptions emphasized architectural possibility and expected performance
upside. Field-validated constraints added necessary realism.
Security hardening timeline. Early framing treated some security controls as
follow-on work that could be deferred until after core functionality and performance
milestones. Implementation experience showed this assumption was too optimistic: de-
laying hardening materially changed deployment risk class and quickly constrained where
and how the platform could be used.
Operational fragility versus benchmark strength. Another assumption was
that strong benchmark outputs would dominate practical value. In practice, operational
fragility often had a larger effect on user experience than raw performance numbers. A
system can benchmark well and still feel unreliable if startup order, recovery behavior,
or configuration consistency are unstable.
Heterogeneity tolerance. Initial planning underestimated how much host diversity
and environment variation would shape behavior. Field work showed that heterogeneous
nodes require explicit tolerance design, strict baseline controls, and clear fallback proce-
dures; without these, small differences between hosts can cascade into large integration
uncertainty.
As a result, the thesis now treats deployment readiness as a multi-axis condition
that includes security completeness and operational reproducibility, not just functional
correctness and speed.
9.5 Practice Evidence Linked to Thesis Chapters
Practice evidence contributed directly to the technical core:
• Chapter4(Architecture): roledecompositionandpath-boundarydecisionswere
refined by implementation constraints.
• Chapter 5 (Implementation): troubleshooting sequences and blocker-resolution
records were built from field operations.
47
• Chapter6(Performance): benchmarkinterpretationincorporatedpracticalcon-
tention and stability context.
• Chapter 7 (Security): mitigation feasibility and control resilience were evaluated
in realistic operational conditions.
• Chapter 10 (Discussion): proven-vs-projected boundaries were sharpened by
real deployment friction.
This crosswalk clarifies that practice notes are not anecdotal filler; they are method-
ological context that improves interpretation quality while measured outputs remain the
basis for final claims.
9.6 Disclosure, Confidentiality, and Bias Controls
Because parts of the implementation context involve industry-facing engagement, this
thesis applies explicit disclosure boundaries. Shared content prioritizes architecture logic,
reproducible procedures, and measured outcomes while excluding sensitive operational
details that are not required for thesis-level verification.
Bias controls applied in writing include:
• separation of measured evidence from interpretive narrative,
• explicit labeling of deferred and unresolved controls,
• and avoidance of commercialization claims beyond available empirical support.
These controls preserve both confidentiality obligations and research integrity, ensur-
ing that conclusions remain technically defensible without overexposing sensitive imple-
mentation specifics.

Industry-context interpretation therefore requires balance. The technical direction

10.2 Revisiting the Research Questions
RQ1: Can PCIe-fabric-based pooling support a decentralized neighborhood
micro-data-center model?
At prototype scale, yes. Chapter 4 demonstrates a working architecture and Chap-
ter 5 confirms implementation under realistic host constraints. The result is not full
commercialization proof, but it is feasibility evidence.
RQ2: What performance characteristics are achievable relative to local-
network and cloud-oriented alternatives?
Chapter 6 shows that the evaluated system can deliver low remote-memory latency
and high DMA throughput in the tested environment, supporting workloads where lo-
cality and transfer efficiency matter. Comparative interpretation indicates meaningful
advantage for selected edge-adjacent use cases, while broad universality is not claimed.
RQ3: Which security and operational risks dominate in shared residential
contexts?
Chapter 7 identifies unresolved authentication and confidentiality gaps as the domi-
nant deployment blockers, with additional operational risks tied to configuration integrity
and fairness under load-abuse patterns.
RQ4: Whatdesignandexecutionpatternsimprovepracticaldeployability?
Chapters5and9showthatfield-embeddediteration, disciplinedevidencetraceability,
and explicit implemented-vs-proposed claim boundaries improve reliability of technical

10.4 Limits of the Current Study
Several limitations define interpretation boundaries.
Scale limitation. Validated measurements are anchored to a prototype-scale deploy-
ment rather than a full neighborhood fleet. This means the thesis can establish feasibility
and behavior under controlled expansion, but cannot yet claim stable system dynamics
under broader multi-site contention and long-horizon fleet growth.
Hardware heterogeneity. Consumer-host variability increased practical realism,
but it also reduced strict hardware-control uniformity. As a result, some observed behav-
ior reflects both architecture properties and host-environment variation, which is valuable
for realism but complicates strict isolation of platform-only effects.
Security maturity limitation. Critical controls for segment authentication and
transport confidentiality were not complete at thesis close. This limits deployment-grade
interpretation, because security completeness is a gating condition for open shared oper-
ation and not a secondary optimization concern.
Operationalinstrumentationlimitation. Somecontrolswerevalidatedinbounded
tests rather than long-duration production-like runs. Therefore, control effectiveness and
overhead should be treated as strong directional evidence in this phase, with additional
longitudinal validation still required.
51
These limits do not negate feasibility findings; they qualify generalization range and
deployment readiness claims.
10.5 Roadmap to Deployment-Grade Systems
A pragmatic path from research prototype to deployment-grade system can be staged as
follows:
1. Security closure stage: implement authenticated segment access and fabric confi-
dentiality controls; re-benchmark overhead and failure behavior.
2. Operational hardening stage: convert manual recovery knowledge into automa-
tion, policy checks, and startup-order validation tooling.
3. Scale-validation stage: expand to larger topologies with sustained mixed workload
campaigns and fairness-sensitive contention tests.
4. Service integration stage: validate application-facing orchestration for pooled re-
sources under user-driven demand patterns.
5. Deployment qualification stage: assess maintainability, compliance posture, and
cost behavior under long-horizon field operation.
This sequence reflects the central lesson of the thesis: architecture and baseline perfor-
mance justify continuation, but deployment quality depends on security and operations
maturity.
10.6 Future Research Directions
Future work should prioritize high-leverage experiments that close the current evidence
gaps.
Authenticated segment governance. A near-term priority is capability-token ac-
cess control for segment operations, including explicit revocation and audit linkage. This
would move trust boundaries from implicit node-level assumptions to explicit, enforceable
authorization semantics.
Confidentiality-performance characterization. Another priority is evaluating
confidentialitymechanismsatappropriatelayersandquantifyingtheirlatency/throughput
cost under realistic workloads. The goal is not encryption in abstraction, but measured
designchoicesthatpreservesecuritywhilemaintainingacceptableperformanceenvelopes.
Fairness-aware abuse control. Queue and rate-control policies should be extended
and tested under adversarial plus bursty mixed-load conditions, with victim-side latency
52
fairness treated as a first-class metric. This is essential for translating partial abuse
mitigation into operationally robust multi-tenant behavior.
Longitudinal scale reliability. Larger-topology and longer-duration studies are
needed to characterize stability, recovery behavior, and maintenance burden over time.
Such studies would improve confidence that prototype-era reliability patterns generalize
beyond short benchmark windows.
Socio-technicaldeploymentresearch. Finally,shared-ownershipdeploymentstud-
ies should examine operator burden, governance models, and trust calibration among
participants. These factors are central to adoption outcomes and should be evaluated
alongside technical performance and security controls.
Collectively, these directions transform the current prototype from a validated tech-
nical possibility into a candidate operational platform.

11.1 Core Findings
This thesis set out to evaluate whether PCIe-fabric-driven resource pooling can support
a decentralized neighborhood-scale micro-data-center model under practical constraints.
The core evidence-backed findings are:
• a functioning prototype architecture was implemented and validated at multi-node
scale,
• measured performance demonstrates low-latency and high-throughput behavior in
the evaluated environment,
• implementation feasibility is real but strongly conditioned by integration and oper-
ations discipline,
• and security posture is improved by implemented controls but not yet deployment-
complete due to unresolved high-severity controls.
The net conclusion is therefore a qualified positive: decentralized PCIe-fabric infras-
tructure is technically feasible and promising, but production-grade shared deployment
requires additional security closure and operational hardening.
54
11.2 Primary Contributions
(1) Empirical systems contributions.
• End-to-end architecture realization for distributed PCIe-fabric experimentation on
non-datacenter hosts.
• Benchmark-based characterization linking resource-pooling design to measurable
communication behavior.
(2) Security and risk contributions.
• A threat and vulnerability model tailored to shared residential fabric contexts.
• A mitigation execution record with explicit status classification and overhead-aware
interpretation.
(3) Practice-embedded implementation contributions.
• A structured engineering narrative that connects troubleshooting cycles to method-
ological decision quality.
• Operational lessons for transitioning from prototype success toward reproducible
deployment behavior.
11.3 Practical Implications
Forpractitioners,thisworksuggeststhatdecentralizedneighborhoodinfrastructureshould
be evaluated as a staged engineering program, not a single deployment event.
Security-gated progression. Early adoption should be conditioned on explicit
security gating criteria before broad multi-tenant exposure. In practical terms, teams
need clear pass/fail thresholds for authentication, confidentiality, and abuse controls so
expansion decisions are based on verified readiness rather than optimistic projection.
Operational maturity and recovery quality. Deployment decisions should also
prioritize operator workflow maturity and failure-recovery reproducibility. Prototype
success is not enough if bring-up, incident response, and rollback behavior depend on ad
hocexpertintervention; repeatableproceduresandobservablerecoverypathsarerequired
for sustained operation.
Workload-fit discipline. Finally, workload selection should focus on cases where
locality and low-overhead data movement provide a real advantage. The strongest early
deployment valuecomes from workloads thatarelatency-sensitive, coordination-heavy, or
data-locality constrained, rather than from broad claims of universal workload suitability.
55
For decision-makers, the practical implication is that architectural promise alone is
insufficient. Deployment readiness depends on whether security controls, observability,
and operational process quality co-evolve with performance.
11.4 Publication Readiness and Target Venues
The thesis materials support a publication split strategy with four complementary tracks:
• Systems architecture paper: decentralized PCIe-fabric topology design, stack
decomposition, and prototype implementation decisions.
• Performance paper: benchmark methodology and latency/throughput interpre-
tation under edge-local workload framing.
• Security paper: residential threat model, vulnerability findings, mitigation out-
comes, and residual-risk roadmap.
• Practice/operations paper: field-embedded engineering workflows, failure tax-
onomy, and reproducibility-oriented lessons.
This partitioning improves clarity, reduces claim inflation, and allows each venue
submission to emphasize the strongest evidence for its audience.
11.5 Closing Remarks
This thesis argues for a middle path between isolated home systems and hyperscale cloud
centralization: localized, high-performance, collaboratively managed infrastructure built
on disaggregated resource principles. The implemented prototype and measured evidence
justify continued investment in this direction. The unresolved controls and operational
constraints also make clear that meaningful engineering work remains.
The contribution of this work is not a claim of finished infrastructure, but a traceable
foundation: what has been demonstrated, what remains open, and how to move from
research feasibility toward deployment-grade reality.
I also want to close with gratitude. I sincerely thank the professors and faculty at
UTA for providing the education and guidance that made this work possible. I am
equally grateful to Dolphin for constant support throughout the thesis process, and to
my family and friends for their patience while I remained deeply focused on study and
implementation. Finally, thank you to the readers who made it all the way to the end of
this thesis.
